fighters.name: Mahatma Gandhi
fighters.tagline: Father of the Nation who led India to independence through non-violent civil disobedience
fighters.bio: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was the preeminent leader of Indian nationalism in British-ruled India. Employing non-violent civil disobedience, Gandhi led India to independence and inspired movements for civil rights and freedom across the world. He led campaigns for easing poverty, expanding women's rights, building religious amity, ending untouchability, and above all achieving Swaraj.
fighters.imageAttribution: Elliott & Fry, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Bhagat Singh
fighters.tagline: Young revolutionary who became a symbol of youth resistance against British rule
fighters.bio: Bhagat Singh was an Indian socialist revolutionary whose dramatic acts of defiance and execution at age 23 made him a folk hero of the independence movement. He was convicted for the shooting of British police officer John Saunders in 1928 and for throwing bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly in 1929. He remains one of the most celebrated martyrs of the Indian independence movement.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Subhas Chandra Bose
fighters.tagline: Netaji who formed the Indian National Army to liberate India by force
fighters.bio: Subhas Chandra Bose was a charismatic nationalist leader who broke from the Congress to pursue armed resistance. He formed the Indian National Army (INA) in Southeast Asia during World War II with the slogan 'Give me blood, and I shall give you freedom.' His death in 1945 remains controversial but his legacy as Netaji endures across India.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Rani Lakshmibai
fighters.tagline: Queen of Jhansi who died sword in hand fighting the British
fighters.bio: Lakshmibai, the Rani of Jhansi, was one of the leading figures of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Refusing to cede Jhansi to the British under the Doctrine of Lapse, she took up arms and became a symbol of resistance. She died in battle at Gwalior in June 1858, and British General Hugh Rose described her as 'the most dangerous of all Indian leaders.'
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Sarojini Naidu
fighters.tagline: Nightingale of India — poet, orator, and first woman president of Indian National Congress
fighters.bio: Sarojini Naidu was a poet and political activist who brought eloquence and passion to the independence movement. She participated in the Non-Cooperation Movement, the Civil Disobedience Movement, and the Quit India Movement, being imprisoned multiple times. She became the first Indian woman to be president of the Indian National Congress and later the first woman governor of an Indian state.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Mangal Pandey
fighters.tagline: The sepoy whose single act of rebellion lit the fuse of India's first war of independence
fighters.bio: Mangal Pandey was a sepoy in the 34th Bengal Native Infantry who attacked his British officers on 29 March 1857, becoming the first flash-point of the great uprising. He was tried and executed on 8 April 1857, six weeks before the rebellion spread across northern India. His name became synonymous with rebellion — British soldiers of the era called all Indian mutineers 'Pandies.'
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Birsa Munda
fighters.tagline: Dharati Aba — Father of the Earth — who led the Munda Ulgulan against British exploitation
fighters.bio: Birsa Munda was a tribal religious leader and freedom fighter from the Munda community of Jharkhand who launched the Ulgulan (Great Tumult) uprising of 1899–1900. He mobilised tribal people against the exploitation of zamindars, missionaries, and the British colonial system that had destroyed their forest rights. Arrested in 1900, he died in Ranchi jail at only 25 years old but is revered as a god-like figure across tribal India.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Matangini Hazra
fighters.tagline: Gandhi Buri — shot dead at 72 while still holding the national flag
fighters.bio: Matangini Hazra, known as Gandhi Buri (Old Lady Gandhi), was a 72-year-old widow who became a firebrand participant in the Quit India Movement of 1942. She led a procession of 6,000 people towards the Tamluk police station in Bengal, and continued walking forward even after being shot twice by British police. She was killed still clutching the Indian National Congress flag, her last words reportedly being 'Vande Mataram.'

fighters.name: Chandra Shekhar Azad
fighters.tagline: Azad — the free one — who vowed never to be taken alive by the British
fighters.bio: Chandra Shekhar Azad reorganised the Hindustan Republican Association into the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association and masterminded the Kakori Train Robbery (1925) and the Lahore shooting (1928). He lived by a vow: 'I am Azad, I was Azad, I will die Azad.' On 27 February 1931, surrounded by British police in Alfred Park, Allahabad, he shot himself rather than surrender.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
fighters.tagline: Iron Man of India who forged 565 princely states into one nation
fighters.bio: Vallabhbhai Patel was a barrister and statesman who played a pivotal role in the Indian independence movement and later the integration of princely states. He led the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928 — where peasants called him 'Sardar' — and served as India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister. His diplomatic and at times forceful integration of over 560 princely states into the Indian Union is considered one of the great political achievements of the 20th century.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
fighters.tagline: Architect of modern India and its first Prime Minister
fighters.bio: Jawaharlal Nehru was Gandhi's closest political heir and the dominant figure of the Indian independence movement from the 1920s onward. He was imprisoned nine times by the British, spending over nine years in jail, and delivered the iconic 'Tryst with Destiny' speech as India became free at midnight on 15 August 1947. He served as India's first Prime Minister until his death in 1964, shaping the nation's democratic, secular, and socialist foundations.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak
fighters.tagline: Lokmanya — beloved of the people — who declared 'Swaraj is my birthright'
fighters.bio: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was the first leader of the Indian independence movement to embrace mass mobilisation, using the Ganesh Chaturthi festival and the Shivaji Festival to build Hindu nationalist sentiment against British rule. He founded the newspapers Kesari and Mahratta and was tried for sedition twice by the British. His declaration 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' became a rallying cry for a generation.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Lala Lajpat Rai
fighters.tagline: Lion of Punjab whose murder by police lathi-charge galvanised a generation of revolutionaries
fighters.bio: Lala Lajpat Rai was a prominent leader of the Indian independence movement and part of the famous Lal-Bal-Pal triumvirate. On 30 October 1928, he led a peaceful march against the Simon Commission when police superintendent James Scott ordered a brutal lathi-charge; Rai died of his injuries weeks later. His death directly motivated Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev to assassinate Scott's colleague Saunders in retaliation.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Ram Prasad Bismil
fighters.tagline: Revolutionary poet-martyr who masterminded the Kakori Train Robbery
fighters.bio: Ram Prasad Bismil was a revolutionary freedom fighter and Urdu-Hindi poet who co-founded the Hindustan Republican Association. He masterminded the Kakori Train Robbery of August 1925, in which revolutionaries looted a British government train to fund their activities. Captured and convicted, he was hanged on 19 December 1927 at Gorakhpur jail, composing patriotic poetry until the end.

fighters.name: Ashfaqulla Khan
fighters.tagline: Muslim revolutionary and closest comrade of Ram Prasad Bismil, hanged together in spirit
fighters.bio: Ashfaqulla Khan was a revolutionary poet and freedom fighter who was Bismil's closest friend and co-conspirator in the Kakori Train Robbery. A Muslim from a conservative family, he defied communal divisions to work alongside Hindu revolutionaries for a united India. He was captured after months in hiding and hanged on 19 December 1927 at Faizabad, the same day as Bismil — a symbol of Hindu-Muslim unity in sacrifice.

fighters.name: Sukhdev Thapar
fighters.tagline: The organiser behind Bhagat Singh's revolution, executed at dawn alongside his comrades
fighters.bio: Sukhdev Thapar was the chief organiser of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association in Punjab and a close comrade of Bhagat Singh. He played a key role in the Lahore Conspiracy Case and the hunger strikes in prison to demand political prisoner status. He was hanged alongside Bhagat Singh and Rajguru on 23 March 1931 at Lahore Central Jail, a date India observes as Martyrs' Day.

fighters.name: Shivaram Rajguru
fighters.tagline: Sharpshooter revolutionary executed alongside Bhagat Singh, youngest of the three martyrs
fighters.bio: Shivaram Hari Rajguru was an Indian revolutionary who was part of the team that shot British police officer John Saunders in 1928 to avenge the death of Lala Lajpat Rai. A skilled marksman, Rajguru was the youngest of the Lahore Conspiracy Case trio and was deeply influenced by the Arya Samaj and revolutionary literature. He was hanged at Lahore Central Jail on 23 March 1931.

fighters.name: Khudiram Bose
fighters.tagline: At just 18, one of the youngest martyrs to be hanged in the independence movement
fighters.bio: Khudiram Bose was a Bengali revolutionary who threw a bomb at the carriage of Magistrate Kingsford in Muzaffarpur in April 1908, targeting a judge known for harsh sentences against nationalists. The bomb accidentally killed two British women; Bose was captured while fleeing and hanged on 11 August 1908, just 18 years and 8 months old. He went to the gallows smiling, and his face became an icon on handloom cloth worn by Bengali youth.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Udham Singh
fighters.tagline: Waited 21 years to avenge Jallianwala Bagh, then walked calmly to the gallows
fighters.bio: Udham Singh witnessed the Jallianwala Bagh massacre as a teenager in 1919 and devoted the next two decades to avenging it. On 13 March 1940, he shot and killed Michael O'Dwyer — the former Lieutenant Governor of Punjab who had approved Dyer's order — at a London hall. He was tried, convicted, and hanged on 31 July 1940 at Pentonville Prison, refusing to show remorse.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Batukeshwar Dutt
fighters.tagline: Threw bombs in Parliament with Bhagat Singh to make the deaf hear the voice of the people
fighters.bio: Batukeshwar Dutt was the companion of Bhagat Singh who threw smoke bombs (not intended to kill) in the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi on 8 April 1929, along with leaflets declaring 'It takes a loud noise to make the deaf hear.' He was sentenced to transportation for life but survived — unlike many of his comrades — and lived to see India's independence. He was the last of the Lahore Conspiracy defendants still living at the time of his death.

fighters.name: Bipin Chandra Pal
fighters.tagline: Fire-brand orator of the Lal-Bal-Pal trio who preached aggressive nationalism
fighters.bio: Bipin Chandra Pal was one of the architects of the Swadeshi Movement of 1905 and a member of the famous Lal-Bal-Pal triumvirate alongside Lala Lajpat Rai and Bal Gangadhar Tilak. A gifted orator and journalist, he advocated complete independence (Purna Swaraj) long before it became Congress policy, and was imprisoned for refusing to testify against Tilak. He was one of the first nationalists to argue that Indians must govern themselves entirely.

fighters.name: Gopal Krishna Gokhale
fighters.tagline: Gandhi's political mentor and the great moderate liberal of the independence movement
fighters.bio: Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a social reformer and political leader who served as Gandhi's political mentor and guru. He founded the Servants of India Society to train selfless workers for national service and worked tirelessly within constitutional means to advance Indian interests in the Imperial Legislative Council. Gandhi credited Gokhale with teaching him the importance of social service and patient political work.

fighters.name: Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
fighters.tagline: Youngest Congress president and a passionate voice for Hindu-Muslim unity
fighters.bio: Abul Kalam Azad was an Islamic scholar, journalist, and senior leader of the Indian National Congress who became Congress president at just 35 — the youngest ever. A fierce opponent of Partition, he argued throughout the 1940s that Hindus and Muslims formed one people. After independence he served as India's first Education Minister, laying the foundations of the IIT system.

fighters.name: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan
fighters.tagline: Frontier Gandhi who raised a 100,000-strong non-violent Pashtun army against the British
fighters.bio: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, known as the Frontier Gandhi or Bacha Khan, founded the Khudai Khidmatgar (Servants of God) movement — a 100,000-strong non-violent army of Pashtun men and women on India's North-West Frontier. A close ally of Gandhi, he spent over 27 years in prison across British and Pakistani jails. He remained committed to non-violence in one of the most martial cultures on earth.

fighters.name: Dadabhai Naoroji
fighters.tagline: Grand Old Man of India who first proved mathematically that the British were draining India's wealth
fighters.bio: Dadabhai Naoroji was a statesman, scholar, and one of the founding members of the Indian National Congress. He developed the 'Drain Theory' — the economic argument that British rule was systematically impoverishing India by extracting its wealth — in his landmark work 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India.' He was the first Asian to be elected to the British Parliament (1892) and used that platform to advocate for Indian self-governance.

fighters.name: Annie Besant
fighters.tagline: British-born activist who founded the Home Rule League and became Congress president in India
fighters.bio: Annie Besant was a British socialist and Theosophist who made India her home and became one of the most energetic voices for Indian self-rule. In 1916 she founded the All India Home Rule League alongside Tilak, demanding dominion status for India. She was interned by the British in 1917, which paradoxically made her more popular, and was elected president of the Indian National Congress the same year.

fighters.name: C. Rajagopalachari
fighters.tagline: Rajaji — Gandhi's close ally and India's last Governor-General
fighters.bio: Chakravarti Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) was a lawyer, writer, and independence activist who was Gandhi's closest political ally in South India. He participated in the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Dandi March and was one of the few Congress leaders to initially oppose the Quit India Movement on strategic grounds. After independence he served as the last Governor-General of India (1948–1950) and later founded the Swatantra Party.

fighters.name: Aruna Asaf Ali
fighters.tagline: Grand Old Lady of Independence — hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank when all leaders were arrested
fighters.bio: Aruna Asaf Ali was one of the bravest women of the Quit India Movement of 1942. When Gandhi, Nehru, and other Congress leaders were arrested within hours of the movement's launch, it was Aruna who hoisted the Congress flag at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay, formally starting the open defiance. She went underground for four years, evading police while continuing to organise resistance.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Kasturba Gandhi
fighters.tagline: Ba — who quietly walked beside Gandhi into every campaign and every prison cell
fighters.bio: Kasturba Gandhi, known as Ba (mother), was far more than Gandhi's wife — she was a freedom fighter in her own right. She participated in the satyagrahas in South Africa and India, was imprisoned multiple times, and led protests in Gandhi's absence. She died in detention at Aga Khan Palace, Pune in 1944 while serving the last of many imprisonments, having never sought personal recognition.

fighters.name: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit
fighters.tagline: Diplomat, freedom fighter, and the first woman to preside over the UN General Assembly
fighters.bio: Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit, Nehru's sister, was imprisoned three times during the independence movement and served in the interim government. After independence she became India's first female cabinet minister and one of its most distinguished diplomats, serving as ambassador to the Soviet Union, the US, and the UK. In 1953 she became the first woman to serve as president of the United Nations General Assembly.

fighters.name: Usha Mehta
fighters.tagline: At 22, ran the secret Congress Radio that broadcast Gandhi's messages while leaders were in jail
fighters.bio: Usha Mehta was a Gandhian activist who, during the Quit India Movement of 1942, secretly established and operated the Congress Radio — an underground broadcast station that kept the movement's message alive after all Congress leaders were arrested. She ran the station for about three months before being arrested; the British sentenced her to four years in prison. She later became a professor and lifelong Gandhian.

fighters.name: Pritilata Waddedar
fighters.tagline: First woman to lead an armed raid in India's independence movement — died by her own hand at 21
fighters.bio: Pritilata Waddedar was a Bengali revolutionary who trained under Surya Sen (Masterda) and led the Pahartali European Club raid on 23 September 1932 — the first armed action led by a woman in the Indian independence movement. The raid targeted a club that displayed a sign reading 'Dogs and Indians not allowed.' Shot and wounded during the attack, she swallowed cyanide rather than be captured.

fighters.name: Kalpana Dutta
fighters.tagline: Chittagong revolutionary who fought alongside Masterda Surya Sen in the jungles of Bengal
fighters.bio: Kalpana Dutta was a revolutionary from Chittagong who joined Surya Sen's Indian Republican Army and participated in the Chittagong Armoury Raid of 1930. She spent years evading British police, living in the jungle and carrying arms. Captured in 1933, she was sentenced to transportation for life, reduced on appeal, and released in 1939 after Gandhi interceded; she later married the communist leader P. C. Joshi.

fighters.name: Kamala Nehru
fighters.tagline: Nehru's wife who led the salt satyagraha and picket lines while battling tuberculosis
fighters.bio: Kamala Nehru was an active participant in the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Civil Disobedience Movement, leading women's groups to boycott foreign cloth and picket liquor shops. She was arrested in 1930 and again in 1932 while Jawaharlal was in prison. She died of tuberculosis in Switzerland in 1936 at the age of 36, mourned by Gandhi and the entire independence movement.

fighters.name: Tantia Tope
fighters.tagline: The military genius of 1857 who evaded the British for months after the revolt collapsed
fighters.bio: Tantia Tope was the most capable military commander of the 1857 Rebellion, serving as the general of Nana Sahib's forces at Kanpur and later joining forces with Rani Lakshmibai at Gwalior. After the fall of Gwalior he led a guerrilla campaign for nearly a year, crossing rivers and forests to evade a massive British force. He was betrayed by a feudal chief, captured, tried, and hanged on 18 April 1859.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
fighters.tagline: Last Mughal Emperor, reluctant figurehead of 1857, exiled to die far from Hindustan
fighters.bio: Bahadur Shah Zafar II was the last emperor of the Mughal dynasty and a noted Urdu poet who became the symbolic leader of the 1857 Rebellion when sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed him Emperor of Hindustan. Though more poet than warrior, his name united Hindus and Muslims against the British. After the rebellion failed, the British tried him for treason and exiled him to Rangoon, Burma, where he died in 1862 — his grave unmarked for decades.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Kunwar Singh
fighters.tagline: The 80-year-old zamindar who fought the British with a sword and confounded their generals
fighters.bio: Veer Kunwar Singh was a 80-year-old zamindar from Jagdishpur, Bihar, when the 1857 Rebellion began, yet he became one of its most formidable military commanders. He led his forces across Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh, outmanoeuvring British columns at every turn. Crossing the Ganges during a battle, he lost his arm to a bullet, cut it off himself, offered it to the river as a tribute, and continued fighting — dying of his wounds in his homeland just days after a final victory.

fighters.name: Begum Hazrat Mahal
fighters.tagline: Queen of Lucknow who led the armed resistance after her husband fled and her son was captured
fighters.bio: Begum Hazrat Mahal was the wife of Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh, who was deposed and exiled by the British in 1856. When the 1857 Rebellion reached Lucknow she took command, declared her young son Birjis Qadr as Nawab, and led the defence of the city against British forces for months. After the fall of Lucknow she continued guerrilla resistance before accepting asylum in Nepal, where she died in exile.

fighters.name: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah
fighters.tagline: The Light of War — Muslim cleric who became one of the most feared rebel commanders of 1857
fighters.bio: Maulvi Ahmadullah Shah was a Muslim religious leader from Faizabad who began preaching resistance against British rule before the rebellion even began, predicting its outbreak. Dubbed 'Light of War' (Noor-e-Mujarridat) by his followers, he became one of the most effective military commanders of the uprising in Awadh and Rohilkhand. He was eventually betrayed and killed by the Raja of Powain, whose men claimed the British reward money.

fighters.name: Nana Sahib
fighters.tagline: The last Peshwa's adopted heir who led the Kanpur uprising and vanished into history
fighters.bio: Nana Sahib (Dhondu Pant) was the adopted son of the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II, whose pension the British had refused to continue after his father's death. This grievance made him a natural leader of the 1857 uprising at Kanpur (Cawnpore), where he declared himself Peshwa and expelled the British garrison. After the British retook Kanpur and massacred his supporters, he disappeared — his death was never confirmed and he became a legend of resistance.

fighters.name: Uda Devi
fighters.tagline: Dalit woman warrior who climbed a peepal tree and shot down 32 British soldiers before being killed
fighters.bio: Uda Devi was a Pasi (Dalit) woman soldier from Lucknow who formed and led a regiment of women fighters loyal to Begum Hazrat Mahal during the 1857 Rebellion. At the Battle of Sikanderbagh in November 1857, she climbed a peepal tree and used her vantage point to shoot down an estimated 32 British soldiers before being spotted and killed. Her story was almost lost to history — she is now celebrated as one of 1857's most heroic figures.

fighters.name: Alluri Sitarama Raju
fighters.tagline: Manyam Veerudu — Hero of the Jungle — who led the Rampa Rebellion with bows and guns
fighters.bio: Alluri Sitarama Raju was a charismatic tribal leader from the Godavari Agency (Andhra Pradesh) who led the Rampa Rebellion of 1922–1924 against the British. He combined Gandhi's Non-Cooperation ideology with armed guerrilla resistance, organising tribal Koya people who had been stripped of their traditional rights to shift cultivation in the forests. He raided British armouries for weapons, evaded the British for two years, and was captured and shot dead in 1923.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Komaram Bheem
fighters.tagline: Jal Jangal Zameen — Water, Forest, Land — the battle cry of the Gond freedom fighter
fighters.bio: Komaram Bheem was a Gond tribal leader from Adilabad (Telangana) who organised his people against the Nizam of Hyderabad's forest policies that denied tribals access to their ancestral lands. His battle cry 'Jal, Jangal, Zameen' (Water, Forest, Land) captured the essence of tribal rights struggles that persist to this day. He was ambushed and killed by Nizam's forces in 1940; his story inspired generations of tribal rights movements.

fighters.name: Veerapandiya Kattabomman
fighters.tagline: Polygar chieftain who defied the British East India Company a century before 1857
fighters.bio: Veerapandiya Kattabomman was the chieftain (Polygar) of Panchalankurichi in Tamil Nadu who refused to pay tribute to the British East India Company and openly defied their authority. He attacked a British collector's entourage and engaged Company forces in battle in 1799. He was eventually captured after his brother Oomaturai's betrayal, tried in a summary court, and hanged on 16 October 1799 — one of the earliest figures to take up arms against British rule in India.

fighters.name: Tilka Manjhi
fighters.tagline: The first arrow of resistance — Santali archer who attacked the British before 1857
fighters.bio: Tilka Manjhi (also called Jabra Paharia) was a Santali tribal leader from the Rajmahal Hills of present-day Jharkhand who led the first recorded tribal uprising against British colonialism in 1778–85. He shot and killed the British Collector Augustus Cleveland with an arrow during a battle at Bhagalpur. Captured after years of guerrilla resistance, he was tied to a horse and dragged through Bhagalpur before being hanged from a banyan tree.

fighters.name: Sidho-Kanhu Murmu
fighters.tagline: Brothers who led 10,000 Santals in the first great tribal uprising — the Santhal Hul of 1855
fighters.bio: Sidho and Kanhu Murmu were Santali brothers who led the Santhal Hul (rebellion) of 1855–56 — the largest peasant uprising before 1857. They raised an army of over 10,000 Santals against zamindars and British-backed moneylenders who had reduced the Santali people to debt bondage. Both brothers were killed suppressing the rebellion; estimates of Santali dead range from 15,000 to 25,000. The Hul is still celebrated in Jharkhand and West Bengal.

fighters.name: Pazhassi Raja
fighters.tagline: Kerala Simham — Lion of Kerala — who waged guerrilla war against the British for a decade
fighters.bio: Kerala Varma Pazhassi Raja was the chieftain of the Kottayam kingdom (northern Kerala) who waged a protracted guerrilla campaign against the British East India Company from 1793 to 1805, using the dense forests and local tribal fighters to outmanoeuvre superior British forces. He was never captured in battle — his death came when he was surrounded and killed near Mavilanthode. The British, who called him 'the most dangerous enemy in Malabar,' gave him a ceremonial burial.

fighters.name: Captain Lakshmi Sahgal
fighters.tagline: Doctor who became the commander of the Rani of Jhansi Regiment — the INA's all-women unit
fighters.bio: Lakshmi Sahgal was a doctor in Singapore who joined Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army and commanded the Rani of Jhansi Regiment, the INA's all-women combat unit. She was captured by the British at the end of World War II and tried — the INA trials of 1945–46 sparked massive protests across India and accelerated the British departure. She returned to India and practised medicine in Kanpur for the rest of her life, running a free clinic for the poor.

fighters.name: Shah Nawaz Khan
fighters.tagline: INA officer whose trial in the Red Fort electrified the nation and rattled the British
fighters.bio: Shah Nawaz Khan was a senior officer in the Indian National Army who surrendered with the INA at Rangoon and was put on trial at the Red Fort in Delhi in 1945. The public INA trials — intended to discredit the INA — instead turned the accused into national heroes; Khan was defended by Nehru himself. Acquitted of all charges, he later became a Congress Member of Parliament and remained an important voice for ex-INA veterans.

fighters.name: Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon
fighters.tagline: INA officer whose Red Fort trial alongside Shah Nawaz Khan and Prem Sahgal shook British India
fighters.bio: Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon was a Sikh officer in the British Indian Army who joined the INA after being captured at Singapore. He was one of the three INA officers — along with Shah Nawaz Khan and P. K. Sahgal — tried at the famous Red Fort INA trials of 1945. The decision to prosecute them backfired spectacularly on the British, causing naval mutinies and public demonstrations, and was later cited as a key factor in hastening independence.

fighters.name: Prem Kumar Sahgal
fighters.tagline: INA colonel at the centre of the Red Fort trials that ignited India against British rule
fighters.bio: Prem Kumar Sahgal was a colonel in the Indian National Army and one of three officers tried at the famous Red Fort INA trials of 1945. Defended by Nehru, Bhulabhai Desai, and other Congress lawyers, the trial became a landmark moment in the independence struggle as courts-martial evidence revealed the INA's selfless patriotism rather than treachery. He later married Lakshmi Sahgal and settled in Kanpur.

fighters.name: Mohan Singh
fighters.tagline: The founding commander of the first Indian National Army formed from POWs in Malaya
fighters.bio: Mohan Singh was a captain in the British Indian Army who, after being captured by the Japanese at Singapore in 1942, founded the first Indian National Army in Malaya. He negotiated with Japanese authorities to form an independent force to fight for India's freedom, recruiting from among Indian POWs. Disagreements with the Japanese over the INA's independence led to his arrest; Subhas Chandra Bose later rebuilt the INA under his own command.

fighters.name: Janaki Thevar
fighters.tagline: INA officer and Tamil commander who fought on the Burma front
fighters.bio: Janaki Thevar was an officer in Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army who participated in combat operations in Burma and the Imphal-Kohima campaign of 1944. He led Tamil and South Indian soldiers in the INA's campaigns and survived capture and subsequent British detention. He later became a prominent political figure in Tamil Nadu and was known for his lifelong commitment to Tamil rights.

fighters.name: B. R. Ambedkar
fighters.tagline: Father of the Indian Constitution who fought for Dalit rights alongside the freedom struggle
fighters.bio: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was a jurist, economist, and social reformer who faced caste discrimination from childhood yet earned multiple doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics. He chaired the committee that drafted the Indian Constitution and fought to include fundamental rights that would protect Dalits, women, and minorities. He converted to Buddhism weeks before his death as a final rejection of the caste system.
fighters.imageAttribution: Unknown photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

fighters.name: Periyar E. V. Ramasamy
fighters.tagline: Thanthai Periyar — Father Periyar — who fought caste, religion, and patriarchy with equal ferocity
fighters.bio: Erode Venkatappa Ramasamy, known as Periyar, was a Tamil social reformer and rationalist who founded the Self-Respect Movement and the Dravidian political movement. He resigned from the Congress in 1925 after witnessing untouchability being practised at a Congress-run ashram. He opposed Hindi imposition, Brahminic dominance, and religious superstition throughout his life, and his ideas laid the foundation for Tamil Nadu's social justice politics.

fighters.name: Subramania Bharati
fighters.tagline: Tamil nationalist poet whose songs became the hymns of India's freedom movement in the south
fighters.bio: Subramania Bharati was a Tamil poet, journalist, and independence activist whose passionate verse galvanised nationalist feeling in South India. He wrote prolifically about freedom, women's rights, and social reform, and his song 'Vande Mataram' translation became widely sung. Declared an absconder by the British for his articles in the nationalist journal India, he lived in French Pondicherry for years before being arrested.

fighters.name: Bibi Gulab Kaur
fighters.tagline: Punjabi revolutionary who smuggled weapons from Manila to fund India's independence
fighters.bio: Bibi Gulab Kaur was a Sikh woman activist associated with the Ghadar Movement who worked in Manila, Philippines to spread revolutionary literature and assist in the transport of arms and funds to India. She accompanied Indian revolutionaries on the Komagata Maru episode and faced imprisonment on her return to India. She spent years in jail for her revolutionary activities and is considered one of the few women of the Ghadar Movement.

fighters.name: Prafulla Chaki
fighters.tagline: Threw a bomb at the 'Hanging Judge' Kingsford alongside Khudiram Bose
fighters.bio: Prafulla Chaki was a Bengali revolutionary who, alongside Khudiram Bose, attempted to assassinate District Magistrate Kingsford in Muzaffarpur in 1908. After the failed assassination and the tragic death of two British women in the bombing, Chaki was tracked by police to Mokameh Ghat, Bihar, where he shot himself rather than be captured. He was only 20 years old at the time of his death.

fighters.name: Madan Lal Dhingra
fighters.tagline: Shot a British India Office official in London and went to the gallows quoting love of the motherland
fighters.bio: Madan Lal Dhingra was a Punjabi student in London who, influenced by V.D. Savarkar's revolutionary circle, assassinated Sir William Hutt Curzon Wyllie at the Imperial Institute on 1 July 1909. His statement at trial — declaring that all Indians under British rule had a duty to resist — was suppressed by British authorities. He was hanged at Pentonville Prison on 17 August 1909, one of the earliest Indian revolutionaries to act on British soil.

fighters.name: Kartar Singh Sarabha
fighters.tagline: A 19-year-old revolutionary hanged by the British — Bhagat Singh's lifelong hero
fighters.bio: Kartar Singh Sarabha was a young Punjabi revolutionary and a key leader of the Ghadar Movement who returned from California in 1914 to participate in a planned armed uprising against British rule. The conspiracy was betrayed and Sarabha was arrested, tried, and hanged on 16 November 1915 at the age of 19. Bhagat Singh kept a photograph of Sarabha in his pocket and called him his 'hero and teacher.'

fighters.name: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar
fighters.tagline: Veer Savarkar — revolutionary, lawyer, and theorist of Hindutva — sentenced to 50 years on the Cellular Jail
fighters.bio: V. D. Savarkar was a revolutionary activist who organised arms smuggling networks in India and London and wrote the first history of 1857 as a War of Independence. Convicted of waging war against the King, he was transported to the Cellular Jail (Kala Pani) in the Andaman Islands, sentenced to 50 years — one of the harshest sentences in the independence movement. He later developed the philosophy of Hindutva and became a controversial figure in Indian political thought.

fighters.name: Lala Har Dayal
fighters.tagline: Founded the Ghadar Party in San Francisco to organise Indian labourers for armed revolution
fighters.bio: Lala Har Dayal was a scholar and revolutionary who, after stints at Oxford and Stanford, founded the Ghadar Party in San Francisco in 1913 to organise Indian immigrant labourers in North America for a planned armed uprising in India. The party published the Ghadar newspaper in several Indian languages and attempted a rebellion during World War I that was suppressed by the British. Har Dayal spent the rest of his life in exile in Europe and the US.

fighters.name: Masterda Surya Sen
fighters.tagline: Masterda — who led the Chittagong Armoury Raid and hoisted the Indian flag before the British retook it
fighters.bio: Surya Sen was a schoolteacher from Chittagong (now Bangladesh) who led the Indian Republican Army and organised the Chittagong Armoury Raid of 18 April 1930 — a coordinated attack on the British armouries and telegraph offices in the city. The raid briefly succeeded and his group hoisted the Indian National Flag over the armoury before being forced to flee into the hills. He evaded capture for nearly three years before being betrayed, and was executed on 12 January 1934.

fighters.name: Tipu Sultan
fighters.tagline: Tiger of Mysore — who died defending his capital rather than surrender to the British
fighters.bio: Tipu Sultan was the ruler of Mysore who became one of the most formidable opponents of the British East India Company. He fought four Anglo-Mysore Wars, introduced rocket artillery to Indian warfare, developed trade and technology, and sought alliances with France and the Ottoman Empire against the British. He died fighting at the Fall of Seringapatam on 4 May 1799, refusing all offers of negotiated surrender.

fighters.name: Bhikaji Cama
fighters.tagline: Unfurled India's first national flag at an international socialist congress in Stuttgart in 1907
fighters.bio: Bhikaji Rustom Cama was a Paris-based revolutionary who dedicated her life to the cause of Indian independence from abroad. On 22 August 1907, she dramatically unfurled a version of the Indian national flag at the International Socialist Congress in Stuttgart, Germany — the first time an Indian flag was raised on foreign soil. She published revolutionary literature, raised funds, and worked with Shyamji Krishna Varma and V. D. Savarkar in exile.

fighters.name: Shyamji Krishna Varma
fighters.tagline: Founded India House in London — the revolutionary nerve centre of Indian nationalism in Britain
fighters.bio: Shyamji Krishna Varma was a barrister and revolutionary who founded India House in London in 1905 as a centre for Indian students and independence activists. The house became a hotbed of revolutionary activity, nurturing V. D. Savarkar, Madan Lal Dhingra, and others. He published the journal The Indian Sociologist and spent decades in exile in France and Switzerland, never returning to India; his ashes were brought home 80 years after his death.

fighters.name: Rabindranath Tagore
fighters.tagline: Nobel laureate who renounced his British knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh
fighters.bio: Rabindranath Tagore was a poet, philosopher, and Nobel laureate who played a significant role in the cultural dimension of the independence movement. He composed 'Jana Gana Mana' (now India's national anthem) and 'Amar Sonar Bangla' (Bangladesh's national anthem). In 1919, horrified by the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, he wrote to the Viceroy renouncing his British knighthood — one of the most powerful symbolic acts of the era.

fighters.name: Laxmibai Kelkar
fighters.tagline: Mausiji — Aunty — who founded Rashtra Sevika Samiti to bring women into national service
fighters.bio: Laxmibai Kelkar founded the Rashtra Sevika Samiti in 1936, a women's organisation focused on physical training, social service, and nation building. A widow at 39 with eight children, she was inspired by meeting Gandhi and later by the work of the RSS. Her organisation trained thousands of women in self-defence, first aid, and community service, creating a parallel women's wing of Hindu nationalist activity.

fighters.name: Pushpalata Das
fighters.tagline: Assamese leader who led the assault on Guwahati police armoury during the Quit India Movement
fighters.bio: Pushpalata Das was an Assamese freedom fighter and social reformer who led a significant action during the Quit India Movement of 1942, organising and participating in the attack on the Guwahati Treasury and police armoury. She was imprisoned multiple times for her activities and became one of Assam's most respected post-independence political figures. She spent her later years working for women's rights and the welfare of tea garden workers.

fighters.name: Sucheta Kripalani
fighters.tagline: Sang Vande Mataram before the Constituent Assembly — first woman Chief Minister of an Indian state
fighters.bio: Sucheta Kripalani was a freedom fighter and politician who participated in the Quit India Movement and was imprisoned. She is best remembered for singing Vande Mataram at the historic Constituent Assembly on the midnight of 15 August 1947. After independence she became the first woman Chief Minister of any Indian state, serving as the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh from 1963 to 1967.

fighters.name: K. M. Munshi
fighters.tagline: Gujarati writer and statesman who co-drafted the Indian Constitution and founded the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan
fighters.bio: Kanaiyalal Maneklal Munshi was a Gujarati writer, lawyer, and statesman who participated in the Non-Cooperation Movement and the Bardoli Satyagraha. He was a member of the Constituent Assembly and played a role in drafting the Indian Constitution. He later served as Agriculture Minister under Nehru and founded the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan cultural organisation.

fighters.name: C. F. Andrews
fighters.tagline: Deenabandhu — Friend of the Poor — the British clergyman who became a champion of Indian freedom
fighters.bio: Charles Freer Andrews was a British Anglican missionary who became one of Gandhi's closest friends and spent his life fighting for Indian rights. Known as Deenabandhu (Friend of the Poor), he campaigned against indentured labour in Fiji and South Africa and advocated for India's independence within British Christian circles. Gandhi credited him as one of the few Englishmen who truly understood the soul of India.

fighters.name: Shanti Ghosh
fighters.tagline: School girl who shot a British district magistrate at 14 — one of Bengal's youngest revolutionaries
fighters.bio: Shanti Ghosh was a 14-year-old schoolgirl from Comilla (Bengal) who, along with her classmate Suniti Choudhury, shot and killed the British District Magistrate C. G. B. Stevens on 14 December 1931. Both girls were tried and convicted; Shanti received a life sentence commuted on account of her age. Released in 1939, she later became a teacher and social activist.

fighters.name: Suniti Choudhury
fighters.tagline: At 15, helped assassinate a British magistrate and spent years in prison for Bengal's freedom
fighters.bio: Suniti Choudhury was a 15-year-old student who, together with Shanti Ghosh, shot and killed British District Magistrate Stevens in Comilla in 1931. Both girls were members of a revolutionary group inspired by Surya Sen. Convicted and imprisoned, Suniti was released in 1939 and later became involved in social work and women's rights advocacy in independent India.

fighters.name: Baji Rout
fighters.tagline: The youngest martyr of the independence movement — shot dead at 12 for refusing to ferry British police
fighters.bio: Baji Rout was a 12-year-old boy from Nilakanthapur, Odisha, who worked as a ferryman on the Brahmani River. On the night of 11 October 1938, he refused to ferry British police who were pursuing Congress activists, and was shot dead. He is remembered as the youngest martyr of the Indian independence movement and is honoured by the Odisha government with the Baji Rout state bravery award.

fighters.name: Alluri Sitarama Raju (companion) — Gantam Dora
fighters.tagline: Gond tribal leader who fought alongside Alluri Sitarama Raju in the Rampa Rebellion
fighters.bio: Gantam Dora was a Koya tribal leader from the Godavari Agency who was Alluri Sitarama Raju's most trusted lieutenant in the Rampa Rebellion of 1922–24. He organised tribal fighters, managed guerrilla operations in the forest terrain, and continued resistance even after Raju's death. He was captured and executed by the British in 1924.

fighters.name: Potti Sreeramulu
fighters.tagline: Died on a 58-day hunger strike demanding a separate Andhra state — his sacrifice redrew India's map
fighters.bio: Potti Sreeramulu was a Gandhian activist who had participated in the Salt Satyagraha and Quit India Movement. After independence he undertook a hunger strike demanding the creation of a separate Telugu-speaking state and died on 15 December 1952 after 58 days without food. His death sparked mass protests across Andhra and compelled Nehru's government to create Andhra Pradesh — the first state formed on linguistic lines, reshaping India's entire federal structure.

fighters.name: Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi
fighters.tagline: Journalist-martyr who died in communal riots while trying to save innocent lives
fighters.bio: Ganesh Shankar Vidyarthi was a journalist and Congress leader from Kanpur who edited the Hindi newspaper Pratap and used it as a platform for nationalist journalism and social reform. He participated in non-cooperation and was imprisoned. In March 1931, communal riots broke out in Kanpur; Vidyarthi rushed into the streets to save victims regardless of religion and was killed in the violence — a symbol of communal harmony.

fighters.name: Saifuddin Kitchlew
fighters.tagline: Amritsar's Muslim leader who was arrested the day before Jallianwala Bagh, triggering the fatal protest
fighters.bio: Saifuddin Kitchlew was a Muslim lawyer and Congress leader from Amritsar whose arrest on 10 April 1919, along with Dr Satyapal, triggered the protest march that ended in the Jallianwala Bagh massacre. A close associate of Gandhi, he was a living embodiment of Hindu-Muslim unity in the Congress. He received the Stalin Peace Prize in 1952 and remained a committed Gandhian his entire life.

fighters.name: Bhulabhai Desai
fighters.tagline: The lawyer who defended the INA officers at the Red Fort trials in the most dramatic courtroom in Indian history
fighters.bio: Bhulabhai Desai was a senior Congress leader and one of India's most eminent lawyers who served as Leader of the Opposition in the Central Legislative Assembly. His most famous contribution came in 1945 when he led the defence in the INA trials at Red Fort, turning the prosecution of Subhas Bose's soldiers into a public triumph for Indian nationalism. His eloquent defence moved the public and is credited with hastening British departure.

fighters.name: Durgawati Devi
fighters.tagline: Durga Bhabhi — helped Bhagat Singh escape Lahore disguised as her husband after the Saunders shooting
fighters.bio: Durgawati Devi (Durga Bhabhi) was a revolutionary who played a key role in the Lahore Conspiracy Case by helping Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev escape Lahore after the Saunders assassination, travelling with Bhagat Singh on the train while he posed as her husband. She later attempted to assassinate Lahore's Governor Hailey but the attempt failed. She dedicated her later life to running a school for underprivileged children.

fighters.name: Rani of Jhansi Regiment
fighters.tagline: The INA's all-women combat regiment — first of its kind in Asia
fighters.bio: The Rani of Jhansi Regiment was the first organised all-women combat regiment in Asia, formed by Subhas Chandra Bose as part of the Indian National Army in 1943 and commanded by Dr Lakshmi Sahgal. Recruited from Indian women in Malaya and Singapore, the regiment provided medical support, performed intelligence work, and participated in the Burma campaign. The very existence of an armed women's regiment was a profound statement about Indian women's place in the freedom struggle.

fighters.name: Rash Behari Bose
fighters.tagline: Revolutionary who escaped to Japan and founded the first Indian Independence League in Asia
fighters.bio: Rash Behari Bose (not related to Subhas Chandra Bose) was a Bengali revolutionary who organised the Delhi-Lahore Conspiracy to assassinate the Viceroy Lord Hardinge in 1912 and fled to Japan in 1915 to escape arrest. In Japan he married, became a Japanese citizen, and founded the Indian Independence League and the first Indian National Army in 1942. He later handed leadership to Subhas Chandra Bose and died in Tokyo before seeing India free.

fighters.name: Dhondo Keshav Karve
fighters.tagline: Maharshi Karve — dedicated 60 years to women's education and lived to 104
fighters.bio: Dhondo Keshav Karve (Maharshi Karve) was a social reformer who dedicated his life to women's education and the remarriage of widows — radical causes in 19th-century India. He founded the first university for women in India (SNDT Women's University) in 1916, having spent decades building boarding schools for widows and orphans. The Indian government awarded him the Bharat Ratna in 1958, his centenary year.

fighters.name: Sree Narayana Guru
fighters.tagline: One Caste, One Religion, One God — the spiritual reformer who dismantled caste in Kerala
fighters.bio: Sree Narayana Guru was a philosopher-saint from Kerala who challenged the rigid caste system of the region through his teaching, temple-building, and social activism. His famous dictum 'One Caste, One Religion, One God for Humanity' inspired mass conversion away from untouchability and became a foundation for social reform movements across South India. Gandhi visited him and called him one of the greatest men he had ever met.

fighters.name: Dumka Murmu (Sido)
fighters.tagline: Led the Santhal Hul of 1855 — the great tribal uprising that preceded 1857
fighters.bio: Sido Murmu, together with his brother Kanhu, led the Santhal Hul (uprising) of 1855 in which over 10,000 Santhals rose against the exploitation of zamindars and moneylenders backed by British colonial authority. The rebellion was suppressed with great brutality; Sido was killed in battle. The Santhal Hul is remembered as a precursor to the 1857 Revolt and is a defining moment of tribal resistance in Indian history.

fighters.name: Accamma Cherian
fighters.tagline: Jhansi Rani of Travancore — led a 30,000-strong march on the Secretariat and faced down guns
fighters.bio: Accamma Cherian was a freedom fighter from Travancore (Kerala) who led the historic march on the Travancore State Congress in 1938, walking at the head of a 30,000-strong procession to defy the State's ban on the Congress flag. The Diwan reportedly said she had 'the courage of a man' — she refused the compliment and the patronage. Gandhi honoured her with the title 'Jhansi Rani of Travancore.'

fighters.name: Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani
fighters.tagline: Maulana Bhashani — the Red Maulana who organised peasants across Bengal for four decades
fighters.bio: Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani was a peasant leader and Islamic scholar from Bengal who participated in the Khilafat Movement and the Non-Cooperation Movement alongside Gandhi. He organised tenant farmers against zamindars and later became a major political figure in East Bengal (Pakistan, then Bangladesh). His life bridged the independence movement, partition, and the liberation of Bangladesh.

fighters.name: T. Prakasam
fighters.tagline: Andhra Kesari — bared his chest to a British gun and dared the officer to fire
fighters.bio: Tanguturi Prakasam was an Andhra freedom fighter and lawyer known as Andhra Kesari (Lion of Andhra). During the 1928 Madras protests against the Simon Commission, he bared his chest before a policeman with a drawn gun and dared him to fire — the policeman backed down. He was a close associate of Gandhi and served as the first Chief Minister of Andhra State after independence.

fighters.name: G. Subramania Iyer
fighters.tagline: Founded The Hindu newspaper and made Tamil Nadu's press a weapon of nationalist thought
fighters.bio: G. Subramania Iyer was a Tamil journalist and social reformer who co-founded The Hindu newspaper in 1878, which became one of the most important voices for Indian nationalism. He advocated for women's education, attacked untouchability, and used his journalism to build public opinion against British policies. He resigned from The Hindu to found Swadesamitran, a Tamil-language paper with an even more radical nationalist line.

fighters.name: Rani Gaidinliu
fighters.tagline: The Naga queen who led an armed revolt at 16 and spent 14 years in British jails
fighters.bio: Gaidinliu was a Naga spiritual and political leader from Manipur who joined the Heraka religious movement at age 13 and led an armed revolt against British rule in 1932 at the age of 16. She was captured after a dramatic chase through the Naga hills and sentenced to life imprisonment — Nehru visited her in jail and called her 'the daughter of the hills.' She was released in 1947 and given the title Rani by Nehru.

fighters.name: Senapati Bapat
fighters.tagline: Commander Bapat — learned bomb-making in Europe and spent 14 years imprisoned for the Mulshi Satyagraha
fighters.bio: Pandurang Mahadev 'Senapati' Bapat was a Maharashtrian revolutionary who studied bomb-making alongside V. D. Savarkar in London and was involved in revolutionary activities in the early 1900s. He later became a Gandhian and led the Mulshi Satyagraha of 1921–24, opposing the construction of a dam that would displace thousands of farmers. He was arrested multiple times across six decades of activism and remained politically active into old age.

fighters.name: Damodar Hari Chapekar
fighters.tagline: Pune revolutionary executed for shooting a British plague commissioner — first political assassination of the modern era
fighters.bio: Damodar Hari Chapekar was a Pune revolutionary who, with his brothers Balkrishna and Wasudeo, shot and killed British plague officer W. C. Rand and Lieutenant Ayerst on 22 June 1897 — the day of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee. The brothers were outraged by the brutal and humiliating enforcement of plague quarantine laws that had violated Hindu women's privacy. Damodar was hanged in 1898, and his brothers were executed shortly after.

fighters.name: Jatin Das
fighters.tagline: Died after a 63-day hunger strike in Lahore jail demanding political prisoner rights
fighters.bio: Jatindra Nath Das was a Bengali revolutionary and a member of the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association who was arrested in the Lahore Conspiracy Case and immediately began a hunger strike demanding that political prisoners be treated differently from ordinary criminals. He died on 13 September 1929 after 63 days without food, becoming the movement's longest hunger strike martyr. His funeral in Lahore drew an estimated 200,000 mourners.

fighters.name: Ardesher Cursetji Wadia
fighters.tagline: Bombay labour organiser and Congress activist who built the Indian trade union movement
fighters.bio: Ardesher Cursetji Wadia was a Parsi labour organiser from Bombay who worked alongside Tilak and later Gandhi to build early Indian trade unions. He helped found the Bombay Mill Hands Association and was a key organiser of the 1917 Bombay textile strikes that linked labour rights with the nationalist movement. He was one of the founders of the All India Trade Union Congress in 1920.

fighters.name: Rajendra Prasad
fighters.tagline: India's first President — a humble lawyer who walked barefoot into the freedom movement with Gandhi
fighters.bio: Rajendra Prasad was a lawyer from Bihar who became one of Gandhi's closest associates and participated in every major phase of the independence movement, from Champaran to Quit India. He was imprisoned multiple times and played a key role in organising Congress at the grassroots level. After independence, he served as the president of the Constituent Assembly that drafted the Indian Constitution and became India's first President.

fighters.name: Shaukat Ali
fighters.tagline: Led the Khilafat Movement alongside Gandhi, creating the high-water mark of Hindu-Muslim unity
fighters.bio: Shaukat Ali was a Muslim political leader who, with his brother Muhammad Ali, led the Khilafat Movement (1919–1924) — the most powerful mobilisation of Indian Muslims before Partition. The Ali brothers allied closely with Gandhi and the Congress, creating a brief but genuine period of Hindu-Muslim political unity. Their eventual break with Congress over different visions of India's future reflected the fault lines that would widen over the next two decades.

fighters.name: Muhammad Ali Jouhar
fighters.tagline: Khilafat leader who said he preferred to die abroad than live under British rule — and did
fighters.bio: Muhammad Ali Jouhar was an Islamic scholar, journalist, and leader of the Khilafat Movement who co-founded the Comrade newspaper and allied with Gandhi in the Non-Cooperation Movement. He was imprisoned for nearly three years and spent his later years at the League of Nations and in Europe arguing for Indian Indian self-determination. He died in London in 1931 and, as he had requested, was buried in Jerusalem rather than return to British India.

fighters.name: Vinoba Bhave
fighters.tagline: Gandhi's spiritual heir who walked 100,000 km across India redistributing land from the rich to the poor
fighters.bio: Vinoba Bhave was Gandhi's closest spiritual disciple and a leading figure in the independence movement who was the first individual satyagrahi chosen by Gandhi to launch individual civil disobedience in 1940. After independence he launched the Bhoodan (land gift) Movement, walking across India and persuading landlords to donate land to the landless — collecting over 5 million acres. Gandhi called him his 'spiritual son.'

fighters.name: Shankarlal Banker
fighters.tagline: Millowner who gave up his business to run Gandhi's newspaper and went to prison for it
fighters.bio: Shankarlal Banker was a Gujarati businessman who became a close associate of Gandhi and managed Young India, Gandhi's influential English-language newspaper. He was tried and convicted alongside Gandhi in the famous 1922 Great Trial for sedition arising from articles in Young India, receiving a one-year prison sentence. He surrendered his business interests to dedicate himself to the Khadi movement and constructive programme.
